New story in Calyx Journal!
How do you tell the rich story of an organization like the Berkeley Community Chorus & Orchestra, which has involved hundreds of people over the course of 50 years?
A little over a year ago, the incomparable Betty Pigford, alto, and development wizard for the Berkeley Community Chorus & Orchestra, and my former business partner, Karen Davison (then president of BCCO), approached me about making a short film for BCCO’s 50th anniversary celebration. As we talked, we decided that maybe a film wasn’t quite the right solution. A film would allow us to include only a limited number of voices. Who decides which voices will be heard, which memories and perspectives will be included?
I’ve sung with BCCO off and on for the past 14 years, and was intrigued by finding a way to truly represent the chorus’s unusual history. Founded in 1966 by Eugene Jones — the first African American conductor of a large Bay Area chorus and orchestra — BCCO is now a chorus of more than 200 non-auditioned singers. BCCO performs two major symphonic choral works each year — and concerts are always free to the public.
I’m really interested in forms of storytelling that allow broad participation by the community whose stories are being told. A few years ago, Karen and I spent a fascinating couple of years working with a coalition in East Palo Alto on a community health social marketing project, Get Fit East Palo Alto. By the end of the project, more than 100 people’s voices had been heard, telling often very moving stories about their efforts to gain and maintain good health.
This gave us an idea—and we created StoryChorus, a project true to BCCO’s mission: provide a place where all are welcome to participate, regardless or experience or training. No auditions.
Over the past few months, we’ve developed a project that uses the multiple talents of BCCO’s extraordinary membership. It is hosted online, to make it accessible to the broad community. There are moving tributes to members of the community, humorous memories, reflections on the three music directors, historical photos and recordings, videos, and more. The true heart of StoryChorus are the storytellers who are stepping up with their stories. They are singers, orchestra members, audience members, music staff—people from all eras and aspects of BCCO’s extended family.
So check out StoryChorus to enjoy some BCCO tales. Feel free to contribute, if you’re inspired! Plus, StoryChorus has provided a platform for documenting 50th anniversary events. The fall 2015 concert series was a retrospective of the chorus’s musical history. In spring 2016, the anniversary celebration will culminate in three performances of Benjamin Britten’s War Requiem. You can see, read, and listen to reports on this benchmark year.
A special note of thanks: StoryChorus was built with WordPress, an open source content management system. I had some WordPress experience, but stumbled onto an extraordinary group in Oakland that helped me raise the project to a whole new level: TechLiminal, a hands-on technology coaching for web, cloud, and mobile tech in a fabulous co-working space. I met the extraordinary Anca Mosoiu, founder, at my annual trek to She’s Geeky, the women-in-tech “Unconference.” I’ve overcome my fear of code, and gained a community of smart, creative, and really fun colleagues. Thanks to all of you—Anca, Pieter, Eve, Tumikia, Sue, Nick, Amanda, and the many others who I’m forgetting to list right now! context:Berkeley Community Chorus & Orchestra keywords: Berkeley Community Chorus, Orchestra, StoryChorus, storytelling, community, music, performance, history, voice tags: Berkeley Community Chorus & Orchestra, storytelling, music, performance, history, band, gig, spirituality, event

content:Speaker assistant says: The current state of the world's freshwater resources is a significant concern. Around 2.2 billion people worldwide lack access to safe drinking water, and nearly 40% of the global population faces water scarcity for at least one month per year. The situation has been exacerbated by climate change, which has led to unpredictable rainfall patterns and increased the frequency and severity of droughts.

To address this global challenge, various initiatives are underway to improve water management and conservation. These include:

1. Sustainable agriculture practices: Farmers are adopting more sustainable methods of irrigation, such as drip irrigation, to use less water in agriculture.

2. Rainwater harvesting: Collecting and storing rainwater can help people become more self-sufficient in terms of their water supply, particularly in arid areas.

3. Water recycling and treatment: Recycling wastewater and reusing it for irrigation or other purposes can help conserve resources.

4. Desalination: Coastal regions are investing in desalination plants to convert saltwater into freshwater, although this is an expensive option and can have negative impacts on marine ecosystems.

5. International agreements: Governments worldwide are cooperating to promote sustainable water use and conservation. The United Nations has included access to clean water as a Sustainable Development Goal, and various international agreements such as the Paris Agreement and the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea explicitly address water-related issues.

content:Speaker assistant says: There are several types of bacteria that play important roles in sewage treatment:

1. Aerobic bacteria: These bacteria require oxygen to survive and break down organic matter in sewage. They play a key role in the initial stages of sewage treatment, where they help to remove large organic particles and dissolved organic matter from the sewage.

2. Anaerobic bacteria: Anaerobic bacteria do not require oxygen to survive and are responsible for breaking down the complex organic compounds that remain in sewage after the initial aerobic treatment stage. They produce methane gas as a byproduct of their metabolic processes.

3. Nitrifying bacteria: These bacteria convert ammonia (which is toxic to aquatic life) into nitrite and then nitrate through a process called nitrification. This is an important step in sewage treatment, as it helps to remove nitrogen from the wastewater.

4. Denitrifying bacteria: Denitrifying bacteria convert nitrate back into atmospheric nitrogen gas, which is released into the air. This step is important because excess nitrogen in the water can lead to algal blooms and other environmental problems.

Overall, the different types of bacteria work together in symbiosis to break down and treat sewage, resulting in cleaner water that is safe to discharge into the environment. context:The different types of bacteria work together harmoniously in the process of sewage treatment. They form a complex ecological system known as a biofilm, where different types of bacteria create a cooperative environment within the biofilm. For example, aerobic bacteria use oxygen and generate carbon dioxide, which is then used by anaerobic bacteria. The nitrifying and denitrifying bacteria also work together to remove excess nitrogen from the wastewater. While there is some competition between bacteria for resources such as nutrients and oxygen, this is generally kept in balance by the overall process of sewage treatment. The bacteria have evolved to work together in this environment, and their interactions are finely tuned to optimize the efficiency of the treatment process. As a result, sewage treatment plants are able to effectively treat large volumes of wastewater and produce clean water that is safe to discharge into the environment. keywords: bacteria, sewage treatment, aerobic, anaerobic, nitrification, denitrification, symbiosis tags: bacteria, sewage treatment, ecology, cooperation, biofilm

content:Speaker assistant says: Brewing a delicious cup of coffee doesn't have to be complicated. By following these easy steps, you can make coffee from selecting the appropriate coffee bean to the final stage of pouring it into a mug effortlessly. Depending on your preferred brewing method, refer to the instructions below.

1. Choose the right bean for you

Choose the type of bean that suits your taste. There are many varieties of beans, and each has its unique flavor and aroma. When selecting beans, consider the roast, origin, and freshness.

2. Measure the right amount of coffee

For every six ounces of water, use two tablespoons of coffee grounds. You can adjust this ratio to your liking, but try to keep it consistent for better flavor.

3. Grind your coffee beans

Choose your preferred grind size based on your brewing method. Coarser grinds are suitable for French Press, while finer grinds are perfect for drip and pour-over. Grinding your beans right before brewing ensures freshness and enhances the flavor.

4. Heat water to the appropriate temperature

The ideal temperature for brewing coffee is between 195°F and 205°F. You can use a thermometer or kettle with a built-in thermometer to achieve this temperature range.

5. Brewing Method 1: Drip Coffee

- Place a filter in the drip machine and add the coffee.
- Add water to the machine's reservoir and turn it on.
- Wait for the machine to brew and let it finish before pouring coffee into a mug.

6. Brewing Method 2: Pour-Over Coffee

- Bring water to a boil, then allow it to cool for 30 seconds before pouring.
- Place a filter in the pour-over device and add the coffee.
- Wet the grounds slightly before pouring over a little bit more water and let it sit for 30 seconds.
- Keep adding water slowly in a circular motion until the desired amount of coffee is brewed.

7. Brewing Method 3: French Press Coffee

- Add coffee grounds to the French press and pour hot water over them.
- Mix well and let it steep for three to four minutes.
- Press down the plunger and pour coffee into a mug.

8. Enjoy your delicious cup of coffee!

Pour your freshly brewed coffee into your favorite mug and enjoy it as it is or with your preferred dairy or nondairy options. Sit down, relax, and savor your perfectly brewed cup of coffee. context:memory context keywords: coffee, brewing, coffee beans, coffee grounds, brewing methods, coffee flavor, coffee preparation, drip coffee, pour-over, french press tags: coffee bean, origin

content:Speaker assistant says: Of course, I can provide more detail on how to select the perfect bean for your taste buds. Here are some factors to consider when choosing the right coffee bean:

1. Roast Level

Coffee beans are roasted to different levels, and each level influences the flavor, aroma, and acidity of the coffee. Dark roasted beans, for example, usually have a bold, smoky flavor, while lighter roasted beans are more acidic and have a fruity flavor note. If you prefer a strong, robust flavor, dark roast is for you. Light roast is perfect for those who like their coffee with a light and fruity taste.

2. Origin

Coffee beans are grown in different parts of the world, and each region offers a unique flavor profile. If you like your coffee to have a fruity and floral aroma, consider beans from Ethiopia. Coffee beans from Colombia usually have a nutty and chocolaty flavor. Beans from Central America are known for their bright acidity, while beans from Brazil typically have a smooth and mild taste.

3. Processing Method

Coffee can be processed using different methods, each affecting the flavor profile of the beans. The most common processing methods are washed, natural, and honey. Washed coffee usually has a bright and clean taste; natural coffee is fruity, sweet, and has a heavy body, while honey coffee has a mix of both sweetness and acidity.

4. Freshness

Coffee beans start to lose their flavor and aroma a few weeks after roasting. Therefore, it's best to buy coffee beans that are roasted within the last two weeks. Check the roast date on the bag when purchasing coffee to ensure you get the freshest beans possible.

By considering these factors, you can choose the right type of coffee bean that matches your taste, preference, and brewing method. context:Coffee Processing Method - Honey keywords: bean, roast, flavor, coffee tags: coffee_processing, sensory_experience

content:Speaker assistant says: Absolutely, here's a more in-depth explanation of the coffee processing methods and their impact on the taste of the coffee. 1. Washed Process

The washed or wet process involves removing the fruit from the coffee cherries and washing the beans to remove any remaining pulp. The beans are then dried under the sun or using a machine until the moisture content is reduced to about 10-12%. This method produces a clean, bright, and crisp taste, making it perfect for coffee drinkers who prefer bright and lively acidity in their coffee. 2. Natural Process

The natural process, also known as the dry process, involves drying the coffee cherries with the beans still inside. The beans are then removed from the dried cherries, and the resulting coffee has a fruity, sweet flavor with a heavy body. This process is ideal for coffee drinkers looking for a sweet and fruity taste profile. 3. Honey Process

The honey process, also known as the semi-dry process, is a hybrid of the washed and natural processes. During this process, the skin and pulp of the coffee cherries are removed, leaving some of the mucilage (a sticky substance that covers the beans) intact. The beans are then dried, resulting in a coffee with a sweet and full-bodied taste, similar to that of natural-processed coffee, but with a milder acidity. These processing methods have a significant impact on the taste and aroma of the coffee. Hence, it's essential to understand which processing method produced the coffee you'll be brewing to make sure the coffee's taste matches your preferences. context:Coffee Processing Method - Wash keywords: coffee, processing, taste, cherries tags: coffee_processing, flavor, sensory_experience

content:Speaker assistant says: Yes, processing methods do have an impact on the caffeine content of coffee, as well as its taste. Here's a summary of how the processing methods affect the caffeine levels and taste of coffee:

1. Washed Process

Coffee beans processed using the wet or washed method typically have a cleaner taste and a brighter acidity level. The process usually results in less caffeine content than the natural or honey process. During washing, the caffeine is separated from the coffee cherry's pulp, resulting in a lower caffeine content compared to other processing methods.

2. Natural Process

The natural or dry process is known to produce coffee with a sweeter, heavier body, and often a higher caffeine content. Because the coffee cherries are left to dry with the beans still inside, the beans absorb the sugars and nutrients present in the fruit, creating a fuller, fruitier flavor profile. The caffeine content in natural processed coffee can be higher than washed coffee as it tends to absorb caffeine from the fruits that are still attached to the beans.

3. Honey Process

The honey or semi-dry process is a hybrid of the washed and natural processes. This method produces coffee with a rich, full-body, and less harsh than the natural processing method. The caffeine content of honey processed coffee is between that of washed and natural method coffee.

In general, the caffeine content can vary significantly depending on factors such as the variety of coffee, the region where it is grown, and how the beans are processed, and roasted. It's essential to note that caffeine content alone isn't a reliable indicator of coffee strength, so it shouldn't be solely relied upon to select which processing method to choose. However, the processing method can affect the taste and body of the coffee if you're looking for a particular taste profile. context:This text discusses different methods of processing coffee beans – washed, natural, and honey – and how those methods affect the resulting flavor and caffeine content. It highlights that the processing method significantly impacts both the taste and the amount of caffeine present in the coffee. keywords: coffee, processing, caffeine, taste tags: Coffee Processing, Caffeine Content, Flavor Profile
